intro: Compare how a physical object or a digital interface presents its purpose.
alt: Four product studies show rounded chrome, warm bent plywood, flat graphic blocks and tactile controls.

variants.name: Streamline Moderne
variants.look: A rounded appliance shell and chrome lines convey imagined speed.
variants.history: Streamlining moved from aerodynamic engineering into Depression-era design for trains, products and buildings.
variants.when: Let horizontal lines and a softened profile suggest movement in a stationary object.
variants.why: Horizontal bands suggest a flow continuing beyond the object’s front and rear.

variants.name: mid-century modern
variants.look: Bent plywood, tapered legs and open floor area lighten the workspace.
variants.history: Mid-century designers used forms and materials such as molded plywood to make modern furniture suitable for everyday life.
variants.when: Use thin supports and shaped surfaces to make furniture feel light and practical.
variants.why: Curved plywood can serve as a seat, backrest or shell with relatively little visual bulk.

source.label: MoMA · Design for a New World

variants.name: flat design
variants.look: Broad flat areas and pictograms mark separate levels of information.
variants.history: Digital interfaces in the early 2010s increasingly used graphic color, spacing and simple icon outlines to establish hierarchy.
variants.when: Use simple shapes and spacing when the interface must scale clearly.
variants.why: Without material simulation, color and spacing signal grouping and sequence directly.

variants.name: skeuomorphism
variants.look: Reflections, stitching and raised controls evoke a physical instrument.
variants.history: Early consumer interfaces often borrowed cues from familiar things such as address books, calculators and audio controls.
variants.when: Borrow material cues when a known object can explain how a control works.
variants.why: Familiar textures and raised shapes carry expectations about where to touch.

prompt: Draw a single textless art comparison board for a museum-quality online art atlas. Layout is exactly four square cells in 2x2, edge-to-edge, no gutters or borders; precise, strictly equally sized cells. Order is left to right within each row, then next row. Each cell is a distinct style treatment featuring the same female executive from reference, in original new art. The reference image is for identity only: recognizable ash-blonde hair in neat low bun with four-color windowpane hair clip, black-rimmed rectangular glasses over blue eyes, charcoal sheath dress under fitted black blazer, azure pocket square and blue lanyard with blank ID badge, holding a white coffee mug with a little four-color tile mark. Change the actual render style rather than adding only backgrounds. Layout styles in order: Streamline Moderne: executive reviewing a bakelite desk appliance with rounded cream shell, horizontal cobalt speed lines and chrome trim; mid-century modern product design: warm bent plywood chair and a tapered-leg workspace, mustard and teal; flat design: figure as simple navy, blue and pink vector-like blocks and monoline interface pictograms with zero shading; skeuomorphism: embossed leather panel, chrome controls, real material reflections, stitched seams, raised buttons framing a photoreal portrait of the executive. No readable text, numbers, signatures, words, or extra panels.
